speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question of privilege concerns question No. 2,084 which I submitted and which was answered yesterday. The question is in two parts and reads as follows:
1.	What was the total amount of the budgets of the Department of National Defence for the fiscal years 1949-50 to 1983-64 inclusive?
2.	What was the total amount of actual expenditures by the Department of National Defence for the fiscal years 1949-50 to 1963-64 inclusive?
In replying to the question the Department of National Defence gave the information for the fiscal year 1963-64 but noted that the other information was contained in the public accounts.
I am well aware, Mr. Speaker, that the information is in the public accounts, but I asked the question because I wanted it to be a matter of public record. I checked Hansard and found numerous examples of questions which have been answered with information which is contained in the public accounts, or in departmental reports, or in the Canada Year Book.
Let me quote just two examples. First of all there is question 1,835 which was answered on September 14, as appears at page 7952 of Hansard. This concerns hospital grants paid to the provinces for the past five years. The information is in the publie accounts, but the question was answered. Question 1,793 was answered on September 9 and appears at pages 7776 and 7777 of Hansard. It concerns expenditures on historical sites in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. This information is also in the public accounts, but the question was answered by the department.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is an established practice, and that the ministry should be consistent in this matter.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Just today I read dispatches from Geneva dealing with the news item that appeared in the newspapers and to which my hon. friend has referred. The continuing difficulties in trying to work out a common agricultural policy for the European economic community is one of the most serious difficulties standing in the way of the opening of the so-called Kennedy round. The United States, supported by Canada, has said on a number of occasions that we believe the negotiations should relate not only to industrial goods but to agricultural products. The United States, in negotiations with the European economic community, has not yet been able to agree with them upon a suitable method of negotiation.
However, the discussions are continuing. I think all those concerned-and I believe this includes all the participating governments without exception-would like to see a successful round of trade negotiations. subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege based on my personal interest as well as that of all hon. members of this house.
On October 8 last I raised a similar question to call the attention of the house to the fact that Mr. Maurice Allard, former member of parliament for Sherbrooke, used stationery placed at the disposal of members of parliament to send congratulations or other messages to people in the riding of Sherbrooke and, at that time I read a letter of congratulations for Mr. Robert Delisle, a student at Sherbrooke, who had won a golf trophy.
I thought that this warning would be enough for that former member of parliament who has no right whatsoever to one of the exclusive privileges of members of this house, namely to use the letterhead of the House of Commons to write to their constituents. Now, outdoing himself in rashness, Mr. Allard has convinced Mr. Delisle to send me a threatening letter and order me to return to him immediately the said letter, forbidding me to make copies or photostats thereof, and also asking me detailed explanations on how it came into my possession.
Moreover, the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade), speaking yesterday in the name of the said Mr. Allard on a question of privilege, accused me of a violation of the Post Office Act and told the house that the criminal offence I had committed was liable to a maximum fine of $3,000 or three years in prison or both.
Mr. Speaker, I think the house has already wasted enough time on such a trifle, but due to the way events are shaping, it is my duty to propose that this matter be referred to the committee on privileges and elections.
I am prompted by the following reasons to take this action:
1.	I believe that only members of parliament or officials of this house are authorized to use stationery bearing the crest of the House of Commons.
2.	The use of this stationery for such frivolous purposes as those invoked by the former member for Sherbrooke reflects upon

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in raising his question of privilege, the hon. member for Sherbrooke mentioned having received a threatening letter from one of the addressees who received a letter not belonging to him, and I would ask that the hon. member for Sherbrooke also table the copy of that letter which he qualifies as
[Mr. Chapdelaine.)

threatening in order that the house may have the full story.
As far as the question of privilege is concerned, I should like to quote section 42 of the Post Office Act which reads:
All undeliverable mail and all non mailable matter found in the mails shall be sent to the section of the department established by the Postmaster General for the receipt thereof-
And no other person, even a member of parliament, has the right to intercept, retain or delay delivery of a parcel when he is not the addressee. I hope that this explanation will confirm the complaint I made yesterday.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not object to tabling the letter in question and, furthermore, should the hon. member for St. Mary decide to take legal action later on, he can go ahead.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
I may tell the house that this is not the first time I have heard of this matter, nor does it exactly catch me by surprise.
On October 8 the hon. member for Sherbrooke raised this matter, but he did not follow through with any motion to the effect that it should be referred to a committee for study, and the matter died there. Today, October 22, he raises in effect the same question. As all hon. members know, the proper procedure is to raise a question of privilege at the earliest opportunity. In my view the motion cannot be accepted at this time for at least that one reason, that it has not been raised at the earliest opportunity. The hon. member had an opportunity on October 8 to move a motion, but apparently decided at that time not to follow through.
As partial authority for this view I should like to quote Beauchesne, citation 104, subsection 5, as follows:
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity.
I should also like to quote from Beauchesne, citation 113, beginning at approximately the middle of the paragraph, as follows:
A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy.

In view of the fact that this matter has been discussed now on three occasions it is my opinion that the opportunity for raising this at the earliest possible time was not taken and, consequently, I do not think the motion is in order.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that the second letter I read was returned to me only after October 8 last, and that I did not intend to raise the question by proposing a motion to the effect that the matter be sent to the committee on privileges and elections, even though I have had the letter from the beginning of this week. It is the intervention of the member for St. Mary who, intending to accuse me of having committed a criminal act, tends to lead the house into believing that I have acted illegally.
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the illegal act has been committed by the former member for Sherbrooke, and I should like this point to be elucidated once and for all by the committee on privileges and elections or by the competent authorities, in order that we may know definitely where we stand with regard to the use of House of Commons stationery.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE
speechtext: If any mistakes have been made I am sure they will be corrected. I still hold to the decision that if the hon. member had a point of privilege on October 8-and there appeared to be a prima facie case- he did not avail himself of the opportunity to propose a motion to the house to the effect that the matter be referred to the committee on privileges and elections. Several days, or perhaps even two weeks later, in my opinion, is too late.

subtopic: MR. CHAPDELAINE-LETTERS ON HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY FROM DEFEATED CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MONCTON, N.B.-PROPOSED ENLARGEMENT OF TERMINAL BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it makes it a bit awkward to discuss the estimates of the department when the annual report is not before the house. As I look back at other an-

nual reports I notice that the letters of transmittal signed by the ministers have been dated in the months of May, June or July. In all these years this is the first occasion that has come to my attention of the report not being in the hands of the house by the last week of October. I am surprised it was not available for the standing committee on veterans affairs when they were conducting their deliberations earlier this month.
I should think the minister would have to look into this matter very carefully to see why there has been such a substantial delay. When he first became a minister of the crown in 1963 he signed the report which had been prepared under myself and my predecessor, the hon. member for Edmonton West. He did so on May 30, 1963. What has happened this year? It is almost the end of October and we still do not have the annual report of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I judge that there has been a dereliction of duty here and I hope the minister will improve his attitude with regard to this department.
On December 19 of last year, ten months ago, the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were before the house for consideration. Those estimates had been prepared by the former Conservative government. Consequently we did not spend as much time examining them on that occasion as we are spending in examining the estimates on this occasion, when the estimates are new and have been prepared by the new government.
However, on that occasion the minister had been in office for quite a number of months, and when he introduced his estimates he restricted himself to a very short speech of about three minutes or less. When he introduced his estimates this year he cut his remarks down even more. On both occasions all he really said to us was "The estimates have been before the standing committee on veterans affairs; consequently I have nothing to add to the committee proceedings."
I think this is a wrong attitude on the part of ministers of the crown. When their estimates come before the House of Commons they should make statements indicating what they have been doing during the course of the year, because virtually a year elapses between their appearances for the purpose of discussing their estimates. They should make statements concerning the policy of their departments, tell us what has been done as the result of suggestions made the previous year, and also give an outline of future policy.

We have had nothing of that sort from the minister.
Last December I put three questions to the minister. We accepted the fact that he had not been long in office, and for that matter not long in parliament. But I suggested to him that even then he was derelict in his duty in not giving us some idea as to what he and the department intended with regard to certain matters pertaining to the department. I thought that amendments to the Pension Act should have been looked at, including the question of the benefit of the doubt clause. I also asked him about the section dealing with servicemen now in the regular forces whose affairs come under the jurisdiction of the pension commission. I think it is section 13, subsection 2, but in any event it causes a lot of trouble. I also asked him about the question of veterans hospitals.
The standing committee on veterans affairs also made a report last year containing ever so many recommendations, which the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke drew to our attention yesterday. Not one word was said by the minister with regard to those recommendations of the standing committee. There were 14 paragraphs in the report of the standing committee made on December 12, 1963, but not a word have we had from the minister. He said nothing about the Hong Kong veterans, a question also raised a year ago. I use that as an example because the subject has been aired in the house on two or three occasions in the last few months.
Some members who spoke yesterday said that in view of the fact that the standing committee on veterans affairs had examined the estimates there was not much need to discuss them in the House of Commons. We have recently had a report from the committee on rules and procedure advocating a more extensive use of committees, and there is a general feeling that if problems are referred to committees everything will be all right and the problems will be solved and settled.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that is a careless view of what actually happens. In the years I have been here I have served on a great many committees, and I know exactly what a committee can accomplish and some of the omissions that occur with regard to committees. In looking at the record of the present standing committee on veterans affairs I notice that although it started off with a membership of 40 it found it necessary to reduce its quorum to 10, which is a clear indication the committee was having
Supply-Veterans Affairs difficulty in assembling members to discuss veterans problems.
So I do not see that it makes very good sense for people to say here in the house that these estimates were carefully examined and scrutinized by a committee, which had only four or five meetings, and that on that ground we in our turn should not give much attention to these estimates in the house. I do not take that stand at all. I have had too much experience with committees. It is here in the House of Commons that the minister has to answer to the house with regard to his knowledge of the department and his system of administration. He must also be prepared to give us an indication of the policy of the government and an accounting of what he has been doing.
The minister has been in office now for a year and a half, long enough to indicate whether he is maintaining the Department of Veterans Affairs at the level at which it should be maintained, long enough for him to be able to give us decisions with regard to some of the problems still affecting veterans. In the interests of the general public I think in his opening remarks each year the minister should say something about the veteran population of this country which still requires assistance. People get the wrong impression with regard to our veterans, and that impression should be corrected from time to time by the Minister of Veterans Affairs himself here in this public assembly.
There is a misunderstanding in the country with regard to our veterans hospitals. That situation should be explained again. Granted the minister made a statement last March, I think, but this is the end of October. Let us have a statement now as to the situation with regard to these veterans hospitals.
Why has he not done something with regard to the problems raised by the director of medical services, who last year and again this year in the standing committee on veterans affairs raised the problem of staffing veterans hospitals? In effect, on both occasions he said that although he could manage moderately well under the present terms of reference, it is up to parliament to decide this question for him and give him the necessary direction. If this means we should be building institutions for domiciliary care to look after chronic cases and relieve present hospitals of those cases, then let us have a policy on the part of the work of the department.
The present minister may say, why did you not do that while you were in office? I
9320	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs had this subject under discussion, but I did not have time to complete it during the years our government was looking after veterans affairs. We made ever so many amendments to the veterans charter; we kept the house busy and the officials of the department very busy making the necessary amendments to the veterans charter. We looked after the situation with regard to disability pensions, war veterans allowances and things of that nature. During the years we were in office we raised very substantially the amount of money available for our disability pensioners and those on war veterans allowances. We made it possible for the Veterans' Land Act to operate more effectively by increasing the loans. All told we increased by almost $100 million the amount of money available for our veterans who required assistance. We were repairing some of the neglect of earlier years.
Now, what is this present minister doing with regard to our disability pensioners, with regard to people on war veterans allowances? In the time we were in office we were not able to solve all these problems. There are other problems that arise. Veterans associations right across this country keep bringing forward suggestions for the improvement of conditions with regard to veterans. The department is a good department; we all admit that. It is well staffed. However, the departmental officials themselves require direction. If parliament passes a measure they are obliged to follow the terms of that measure. They have no authority to deviate from it. If there are modifications of the charter that should be introduced, parliament should introduce those modifications.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary to the minister must be frustrated, because in days gone by I recall him as a very active worker in connection with veterans affairs. When he was sitting in opposition he always participated in the debates on veterans problems when we had bills or estimates before the house. He made some very useful suggestions for which I commended him. Some of those suggestions were put into operation later. He must be a very frustrated man now, sitting here as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and we have not heard a word about the suggestions he made two or three years ago. I feel sorry for him because his interest in veterans always impressed me, and I am sure it continues. Where is his influence? Has he no affect on his minister? I am afraid not.


I am not here to praise the minister, as may be evident. I think the minister must show whether he has any value as a minister of veterans affairs. A year and a half has gone by and we have had no declaration of policy from this minister, no amendments to the veterans charter. He talked in the standing committee about amendments he was going to bring forward, but was rather vague and nebulous about them. He said nothing about disability pensioners, nothing about war veterans allowances. He said nothing about the Hong Kong veterans. He has not given us an up to date report with regard to hospitals, and a year and a half has gone by. This Department of Veterans Affairs is not just a department. It has a very important function to perform. I think the department, under this minister, has not received the attention it deserves.
I wonder how the minister fares with his cabinet colleagues. Do they just brush him aside and say "You may have some ideas but we are not ready for them, we have other problems with which to deal." I wonder about his influence with the members of the treasury board. Are they brushing him aside and saying "No, you must not ask for any increase anywhere down the line at all"? Who is responsible for the veterans of this country? The rising cost of living and the vast number of requests that are coming to members of the house mean that the minister must very quickly do something about these particular problems.
I draw these matters to the attention of the committee. I feel the minister should become active so that this department may continue to function at a high level of efficiency and with continuing regard for the veterans of this country. There are still living in Canada over one million veterans of the various wars in which we have been engaged. Fortunately 80 per cent of them do not require assistance, but approximately 20 per cent do. This 20 per cent require help because of wounds suffered in wartime or because of serious economic conditions. We are maintaining our veterans hospitals to look after those who require medical assistance. The department therefore has a continuing responsibility, a responsibility that goes on and on and on.
As I pointed out on one other occasion, once a nation enters into war; once that fateful decision is made, as was done in September of 1939, you are obligated for 70 years to those people who suffer in that war. It is for this reason we are still looking after

some members of the South African force. The disability pensioners of the first world war will still be around for a number of years, although their average age is now about 70. There are hundreds of our veterans who are living to what we call a ripe old age, up into the nineties. They enlist at 19 or 20, so we have a 70 year obligation. The veterans of the second world war will present problems for this parliament and for this country for another 50 years. We cannot brush these problems aside. This is a debt of honour that the country owes to her veterans.
Let me remark again that 80 per cent of the veterans do not require any assistance at all. They are the fortunate ones who escaped serious injury in wartime. We must give help to the other 20 per cent, their dependants, their widows and orphans. I hope the present government will make sure the Department of Veterans Affairs is maintained as one of the important departments over which the government has jurisdiction. I am afraid that in the last year and a half there has been a cooling off of interest with regard to this department and the welfare of the veterans. What I am attempting this afternoon is to draw attention to the importance of reviving that interest so that people generally will have an understanding of our obligation.
The figures in the 1960-61 and 1962-63 annual reports are the most reliable we have, because the annual report for the last fiscal year has not yet been distributed. These show that in 1960-61 first world war disability pensioners totalled 48,000, and their number declined to 41,000 in 1962-63. I may add that I am giving the round figures. World war II disability pensioners numbered 104,000 in 1960-61, and increased to 106,000 by the end of 1962-63. The number receiving war veterans allowances increased from 48,000 in 1960-61 to 54,000 in 1962-63, and these figures show that the decline in the number of first world war veterans is matched by the increase in the attention that must be given to the second world war veterans and the boys from Korea.
I anticipate that with the improved economic conditions over the last 20 years, better conditions than we had between 1920 and 1940, the number of veterans from the second world war who will require war veterans allowance will not reach the same percentage as those from the first world war, who had a much more difficult period in which to adjust themselves. If economic conditions improve and social improve-
Supply-Veterans Affairs ments continue, the veterans' problem will not reach the magnitude it did following the first world war, but I give the figures to illustrate the continuing problem that faces the department.
There is another subject I wish to raise, but I shall not do so now because it is entirely different from what I have been talking about and I see I have almost exhausted my specified allotment of time. However, I conclude by urging the minister to give us a definite statement with regard to what he intends to do concerning disability pensions, war veterans allowances and the Hong Kong veterans, whose case has been ably presented by various members. Also I urge him to give us an up to date report on medical services and veterans hospitals.

Mr. Chairman, one table is entitled, "World war I pensions for selected fiscal years 1920 to 1964". These tables give the number of pensions paid, the annual liability for disability, and then the number of pensions paid to dependants and the amount. Then the total amount is given for the two categories. There is also a second table for the years 1941 to 1964 in regard 
to world war II pensions. This table is on the same basis. Then there is a third table which is, shall we say, a synopsis of the first two tables. This table is entitled, "Total war pensions for selected fiscal years 1940 to 1964".
The conclusions we may draw are that the annual financial liability for pensions increased for nearly two decades following

world war I, rising from $25 million in 1920 to nearly $41 million in 1940. With the granting of pensions for disability or death during service in world war II and with the increase in the basic rate of pension, the annual financial liability since world war II rose from $60 million in 1946 to a peak of almost $148 million in 1958. In 1959 and 1960 a slight decrease occurred as the number of pensioners declined, but the 1961 increase in rates raised the annual liability by $24 million. Then there was a new peak of $173 million in 1962. With regard to 1964, the estimated cost is $168 million. The peak number of pension recipients reached a maximum of 195,900 in 1950 but has been declining ever since. There are now about 177,000 pensioners, of whom 10,000 live outside Canada.
With regard to the first world war I will take some selective figures. It is interesting to note that the peak in the number of disability pensioners for world war I was in 1940, when there were just over 80,000, and there were some 18,000 dependants, for a total of 98,310, with an annual liability of about $40.5 million. By 1945 this figure had declined to 91,000 pensioners, with a liability of $37 million. In 1960 there were only 48,000 pensioners, with some 15,000 dependants, and with an increase in rates the pension liability was some $57 million. On March 31, 1964 there were 38,493 disability pensioners and 14,321 dependant pensioners, for a total liability of $58.8 million. That is with regard to world war I.
So far as world war II is concerned, in 1945 there were 15,506 pensioners and 11,419 dependant pensions for a total liability of $13.7 million. In 1955 there were 100,000 odd disability pensioners with some 18,000 dependant pensioners for a total liability of $71.2 million. In 1960 there were 104,911 disability pensioners and 17,546 dependant pensioners for a total liability of $87.9 million. In 1964 -this is still world war II-there were 106,628 disability pensioners and 16,581 dependant pensioners for a total liability of $107.9 million.
Just as a last recap, according to the tabular information before me, in 1964 there were 176,023 pensioners, including dependants, who served in world wars I and II, for a total annual liability of $166.7 million. As for the Korean forces there were 1,962 pensioners for a total liability of $1.5 million. As soon as I have completed my references to some more statistical information, Mr. Chairman, I will give this information to Hansard.

Yes, they are short tables and will occupy less than one page, I think.
I did speak of war veterans allowance. According to the information I have there were about 54,000 under this head. We know that indigent overseas veterans may also receive free treatment services and other veterans may obtain treatment at cost. I think this information with regard to veterans benefits which has been published by the tax foundation is of considerable interest, and as my hon. friend for Winnipeg South Centre indicated it would be interesting if the minister when he replies could give us a projection forward of the number of disability pensioners including dependants who might be expected by his departmental officials over the next five or ten years. Also some indication of the hospital care required would be enlightening. I remember that the director of medical services indicated there was quite a change in the treatment pattern regarding world war I veterans. There were fewer and fewer active treatment patients with disability ailments or pensionable disabilities, but there was a greater incidence of patients requiring chronic and domiciliary care. None of us is getting any younger and I am sure that the incidence of world war II veterans in the latter two categories has now become quite noticeable both as regards war veterans allowance and chronic and domiciliary care. Certainly men who in the early 1940's were in their forties are today well over the sixties and certainly their presence is now being felt in the patient stream, and over the next 20 or 25 years I think we are going to see the bulk of them.
It is true that much more extensive hospital facilities are available to the population in general through the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, and there may be a lightened load on the Department of Veterans Affairs. Certainly in provinces such as Alberta where there are some very fine senior citizens homes we are going to get much less requirement for domiciliary care. Also auxiliary hospitals are being built in the province in fairly large numbers and this is going to reduce the incidence of chronically ill patients who are under the jurisdiction of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
This pattern is not general throughout the country. It is unfortunate but there it is. I think we should get some sort of forecast from the minister for the next five to ten
3326	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs years-I think it is asking too much to forecast over the next 20 to 25 years.
Another area concerning which I have had quite a conversation with the minister and in which I know he is very interested is this: Could he give the committee some idea of the thinking of his officials in connection with dealing with those men who must leave our regular forces as a result of incurring injury while in service? For example, they may have lost an arm or a leg or an eye or sustained a back injury. Are these men who are injured in the course of duty or while in service in our regular forces to be cast on some sort of scrap heap? They do not come under any workmen's compensation legislation. They are not covered by a pension and disability plan with a private concern such as might tie the case in industry. What are we going to do with them? This is something with which a man is concerned when he enlists, and if we want to continue to get the right type of people in our regular forces we must concern ourselves with this matter.
I do not know whether the present legislation is broad enough to deal with this matter. I suggest that if it has not already been done -I know the minister is thinking about this -a full study should be made to bring this matter into the ambit of another act. It certainly does not come under veterans benefits because these men are not war veterans. The matter does not come under war veterans allowance. I think there should be some other head of legislation to cover these persons because I am certain more and more cases are going to arise. After all, it is now ten years since 1954 when our regular forces were constituted at the level of 120,000. There must be a rather imposing total of these cases, each one becoming harder and harder to deal with. One feels that there should be adequate compensation, but there does not appear to be adequate legislation to cover this situation.
With those few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest to the minister that he give us a full statement when he does reply in respect of the points which have been raised by various members of this house, because I think we would then be in a better position to deal with these estimates. Unfortunately many of these things were not fully considered by the committee.

Mr. Chairman, while I have no intention of making a lengthy speech I do feel that I must speak for a few minutes during our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, because of their importance to so many Newfound-


landers. I am appealing primarily on behalf of the Newfoundland foresters who served during the last world war. I am sure it is the wish of all members of parliament on all sides of the house, as well as of all the people of Canada, that our veterans and their families receive adequate compensation for their services.
At a result of the speeches which have been made in the house in the last two days during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, it can be seen that veterans have the sympathy and support of us all. I should like to express my appreciation to the minister, and particularly to his parliamentary secretary and the officers of the department, for their co-operation and many acts of courtesy in assisting me in dealing with matters which I have had to refer to them from time to time.
I must again bring to the attention of the minister the need to bring the status of Newfoundland veterans in line with that of Canadian veterans, and request that the government take into consideration the services given by the forestry units of world war II, as well as the merchant navy and the rescue tug service. All who served in these bodies should and must be brought under the veterans charter. There is scarcely a week during which I do not have to refer matters relating to Newfoundlanders who served in the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit to the Department of Veterans Affairs here in Ottawa.
During the second world war many Newfoundlanders were asked to serve with the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit and they were told that by serving in this unit they would be performing duties as important as any other branches of the services. Hundreds of Newfoundlanders answered the call to duty and served side by side with the Canadian forestry corps in a manner that reflected credit on them and their province. They were exposed to the same hazards and dangers from invasions and bombings, and for a longer time they were active in the front line of battle, as evidenced by Captain A. C. Hanely for the director of territorial army and army cadet force.
I have heard it said that the commission of government of Newfoundland did not recognize any obligation towards the forestry unit. Surely, Mr. Chairman, this does not mean that the obligation does not exist. The time is long past for the Newfoundlanders who served with the forestry units to receive the

same recognition as other Canadians who served in similar capacities.
I am very well acquainted with many of these foresters because it was my duty to purchase the clothing they used, on behalf of the then Newfoundland commission of government, before they left to take up their duties overseas. These foresters have never been recognized as veterans, as far as I can understand, because they did not wear uniforms.
I should like to quote from a brief prepared on behalf of the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit. At page 10 of that brief the following is stated:
Why did the Newfoundland unit not have a uniform? It is submitted that the only reason is because the United Kingdom government wanted loggers and wanted them badly and fast. There was no time to provide the first contingent with uniforms. It was much less expensive for the government to send them in their own civilian clothes and in fact the men could, most likely, work with greater ease and more comfort in these clothes than in uniform. Two thousand Newfoundland overseas forestry unit men were in Britain by February 1940 whereas the first contingent of Canadian forestry unit men did not arrive there until late 1941 and early 1942.
They were not recruited in the same manner as the other fighting forces, but they did exactly the same work, and for a longer period, as the members of the Canadian forestry corps. 1 feel that the time is long past when this wrong should be rectified, and I hope that the minister will find some way to overcome this technicality, thus treating the Newfoundland foresters in the same manner as other Canadians.
It has been said that Newfoundland foresters did not sign for the duration of the war. This fault in many cases did not lie with the foresters themselves. They were asked to sign up for six months, and this was done, and then many of them signed for another six month period. However, on March 31, 1960, a brief was submitted to the then minister of veterans affairs. In this brief it was pointed out in section 3, clause B, that the contract was altered in June, 1940, when each individual had to sign a formal agreement that he would not and could not be transferred to any other unit or to any of His Majesty's armed forces, and had to sign for the duration of the emergency.
This, Mr. Chairman, shows how important the work of our Newfoundland overseas forestry unit was, and I strongly appeal to the minister, not to show any particular preference to our Newfoundland overseas foresters,
Supply-Veterans Affairs but to see that they are treated in the same manner as other veterans.
I strongly urge the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to the submission made on behalf of the Newfoundland forestry unit. The brief from which I quoted explains in detail why the Newfoundland foresters did not have uniforms. In spite of that fact, they were told that they were doing as important work as the other branches of the services. If the minister will give consideration to the brief which was submitted,
I am sure that the members of our Newfoundland overseas forestry unit will be treated as veterans, and I submit they should be treated in that manner.

Mr. Chairman, as regards the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, I should like to direct but a few questions to the minister, so as to clarify the matter of the pension granted to the veterans and that of paid holidays. I should like to know to what extent the Department of Veterans Affairs is responsible as far as the veterans' protection and welfare are concerned. Exactly where does this responsibility end in the case of war casualties? What kind of supervision can the minister exercise in the case of the veterans' hospitals such as the Queen Mary hospital, in Montreal, and the Ste. Foy hospital in Quebec and also in the case of a veteran's death?
Mr. Chairman, a rather sad case comes to mind. Without belabouring the point, I would like to say a few words about it, in the hope of sparing people the agony which I saw this veteran suffer. This young man had enlisted in the air force, and was sent to Germany. During his stay in Germany, while on leave-probably on a paid leave, because I am not too familiar with the military regulations-he was a victim of a very serious accident and had to be hospitalized in Germany. The next day, he was transferred to a British hospital where he was very well taken care of. During his stay in that British hospital, a telegram was sent to his family, stating his condition. After approximately ten days, when the patient was well enough to be moved-apparently, one or two discs in his spinal column were fractured-the British physicians, in the best interests of the patient, decided to remove him to the Montreal veterans' hospital, after having informed him that he would undergo an operation in that institution and that in two or three months, his condition would be normal once more.
9328	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs
His family was most surprised when they learned that this Montreal hospital no longer recognized those servicemen who came from England but has a French Canadian name. It was in that hospital that this patient endured agony. Month after month, his operation was postponed, and finally it was no longer mentioned. He was termed a "crybaby". After a whole month, and many investigations, the government of the day was informed about the conditions prevailing at the hospital; it ordered an investigation and as a result thereof, two matrons, who came directly from England, and who were the supreme authorities at the hospital, were probably sent back to England. As for our patient, at the end of three months he could not stand it any longer, probably because his wound was getting more infected every day and prevented him from sleeping. He spent his time yelling his head off. So it was decided to put him in a cast from neck to toe. There he remained for three weeks and, when his yells got too loud, they put him in a dark room so they could not hear him shout. Their patience at an end, his relatives went to the hospital. And when they saw the condition he was in, they had the cast removed and had him sent to the hospital in Quebec city. This is where it was found that the flesh was in a state of decay and it was too late to do anything.
Mr. Chairman, the pain that patient had to endure was such that twice he tried to kill himself by cutting his veins open. When he yelled too loudly, they told him: "You go over there in the corner, you dirty Canadian."
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I went to the hospital myself but I must say that at that time the government took the situation in hand and made a thorough cleanup. Now, I am not blaming the department, which did its duty; my sole purpose is to tell you about this case. After two years in the Quebec hospital, that serviceman died.
It is strange that he received only $7 a week during his stay at the hospital. That is the point I especially want to stress before the committee. For three years he only received $7 a week and his family had to send him $10 a week for petty expenses. He died three years later. Upon his death his family was granted $200 and not a penny more. This is worth noting. The family was unable to obtain one penny more. They made various representations, consulted Quebec lawyers,


one of whom was asking $2,000 saying "I will fix this for you". I wonder if the committee and the minister would take this case into consideration, and I ask the minister if the army is still responsible for soldiers on leave with pay.
If the army, through the Department of Veterans Affairs, pays more than $7 a week to a veteran who is ill, why does it only pay $7 per week to a veteran who was hospitalized and unable to do anything since he remained three years lying on his back in hospital?
I have been unable to understand this attitude. I went with his relatives to try to clear up the matter and recover at least the expenses which they had incurred, but we were unable to obtain more than $200 after the death of that veteran.
I know that the government of that day assumed its responsibilities when the veteran was in the Montreal hospital. As a matter of fact, the department, at its own expense, took him over to the Quebec hospital, where he received the care he needed but too late unfortunately, according to the doctors themselves at the Quebec hospital. In fact, they admitted that a surgical operation would have been required at least two months earlier.
This is why I am speaking now in order to let the officials of the minister's department know about the abuses in the army and military hospitals. I am sure that the minister, instead of laughing as some may do, will consider the matter more seriously and see the human side of such an appalling case.

I have no intention of delaying the committee this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, but perhaps if I am allowed to put my question the minister can answer all questions at the same time. I should like first of all to ask the minister whether or not any consideration is being given to increasing the amount of money available to veterans under the Veterans Land Act. I believe that at the moment the maximum amount available is $12,000. At a recent meeting of the veterans affairs committee, we heard evidence to the effect that the cost of the average house to the veteran is something like $12,500. I am referring only to the construction cost. In addition to this the veteran has to pay something like $2,000 for the land required. This means that his cash outlay is considerably higher than it was previously when a house could be built for $10,000. I believe some consideration should be given to these facts, especially in view of the fact the government has

seen fit to increase the amount of the loan available from the Farm Credit Corporation, the farm improvement loans, and under this machinery syndicate measure which was passed a short time ago.
I have had complaints from veterans who find it difficult to raise this larger amount of cash necessary for a down payment resulting from these increased costs. It has been said that less than 1 per cent of the loans outstanding under the Veterans Land Act are in arrears. This is a very good record and compares favourably with the record of the Farm Credit Corporation. This is really the only point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. However, while I am on my feet I should like to add my voice to those who have already spoken in support of consideration for increased pensions. Here again I think the government itself has provided the best evidence of the necessity for this move. They have raised the pay of practically all the categories of civil servants as a result of the increased cost of living. This increased cost of living applies to everybody. If it applies to the civil servants, certainly it would apply to the veteran who is trying to exist, in a good many cases, on a limited pension.
I have nothing further to add, Mr. Chairman, except that I believe the fact the minister has received little criticism in this committee indicates that his department is doing a fairly satisfactory job. I should like to say that my own personal experience has been that I have received full co-operation from the minister and the officers of his department.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that hon. members have the interests of veterans at heart and the minister should understand this. I fully endorse the plea for increased pensions for veterans because we all know that the purchasing value of the dollar has gone down. War veterans should have a greater allowance.
I want to stress one point and that is that the benefit of the doubt now seems to be interpreted by the pension commission in the wrong way. The pension commission seems to think they have to doubt the veteran. I think they have it backwards, and my experience has been that the doubt has not been given to the veteran by the pension commission. I want to bring to the attention of the committee the case of a friend of mine who served in the first world war, and in whose welfare I have a particular interest. He is retired now and is in his late
Supply-Veterans Affairs sixties. He never was sick so far as I am aware, and he never asked for a pension. He did not ask for anything. He was always under the impression that when a veteran was old he could go to a veterans hospital and get fixed up. He went to a veterans hospital and the government of New Brunswick paid for his room, but he had to pay the surgeon $75. This man wanted a hearing aid and I will give you the reason he wanted this hearing aid. He says this:
While serving with the 26th battalion C.E.F. in Belgium in the fall of 1917-
I want to say that this man spent his entire service while he was in his teens.
-while the battle of Passchendaele was being fought in which my battalion suffered heavy casualties, my company went in the line with 145 men and four officers; 16 returned and no officers came out. I was one of the 16 that came out safe. We were forced to hold the line for 48 hours due to relief trouble, with no rations other than for the one day; we were very hungry and tired when relieved.
Then he goes on to say that he was very happy to get out alive, but his happiness was short lived. He says:
I was detailed to go back up the line to carry out the wounded. It was during this trip in that I had the misfortune to have my hearing affected. The time was approximately 2300 hours, very dark; travelling in single file after leaving the main road at Ypres a 15 inch Howitzer fired a shell. This was unexpected and so near that the concussion was tremendous-
He turned around three or four times and fell to the ground, but got out. This incident was not reported. He was deaf from then on.
I	said to him, "Well it is strange this was not reported." He said, "There were a good many things in the first world war that were not reported." I should like to quote further from his letter:
Only the day before this happened I had the pleasure to save another soldier's life, not one of our own battalion but of the 31st western troops that had been buried by shell fire early in the morning and when I came across him it was approximately
II	p.m. He could get air enough to breathe but only his feet were out, lying on his belly at that time. I heard his shoes clicking together, with approximately three feet of earth over him, saved only by the metal covering the Germans used to make their flunk holes.
He took his trenching tool, dug the man out and saved his life. He goes on further:
I had a bag of Mills bombs on my back and the attachment on my rifle as I was in that section in my platoon. I started to drop the bombs over approximately 75 yards. I sent about six bombs in that area and waited for approximately one hour as they had stopped firing soon after 1 had started. I was alone at the time, but the machine section of my platoon was nearby so 1 joined them and told them what I had just done, and the N.C.O.
9330	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs In charge there suggested to have a look and see what had taken place. We made around this mound and found a German machine gun and five dead Germans. We brought the machine back with some ammunition but were unable to make it work so we buried it in the mud-
This man is an upright citizen, he is retired, and he cannot even get a hearing aid. I have taken this matter up with the pension board. I know the minister and his parliamentary secretary have done their best but nothing has happened, and so I am mentioning the case in this chamber.
This man deserves something, and as an example, I refer to another case in which a father wrote to me about his son. He told me his son was a cadet, that he had been hurt in a football game, had suffered a shoulder injury, and he eventually got 10 per cent disability pension. This was a young fellow in his teens. But on the other hand, this old soldier who went through the war, and who never asked for anything, cannot get anything from the pension commission. I believe the benefit of the doubt provision must be changed. In fact I would eliminate it. If a good, honest veteran makes an affidavit his word should be accepted. I know the minister has plans for the veterans, for increasing pensions, etc., but I urge him to remove this benefit of the doubt-

I wish to say something about a point made by the hon. member for Charlotte with reference to the benefit of the doubt provision, and I hope the minister will take note of what his own members are saying.
I cannot thoroughly agree with my colleague on this side who said he felt the minister was doing a good job. The minister has been in office for almost two years and during that time not one piece of veterans legislation has been brought before parliament. When you compare that with what was 

brought before the house while the Conservatives were in power-
Ob, oh.

I will have something to say to you fellows in just a few moments. When you compare that record of performance with what the Conservatives introduced I wonder why any veteran would vote for the party that forms the government.
We had a right to anticipate that the minister would make some reference to the legislation he says he proposes introducing, and I say that more forcefully than some other hon. members because I have been a member of the veterans affairs committee ever since it was established. We have had a very happy committee, and so far as I know no partisan politics have been played in it. We all work for the advantage of the veterans, and my main disappointment is that the minister made no reference whatsoever to the recommendations of that committee. As a matter of fact I am extremely doubtful he will take recognition of those recommendations upon which we in the committee worked so hard and so long.
I ask myself, what is the use of serving on a committee like that, digging into the facts for the minister, if he is not going to take recognition of them? I am not asking him to take recognition of all the recommendations. It is not likely any minister would do that, but we members of the committee have a right to know why the minister would not accept our recommendations. He must have a reason but, as I have said many times before in this chamber, some ministers are captive of their officials. I ask, if he is not going to take the recommendations of the committee, then whose recommendations is he taking? We are entitled to know that.
Why is it that veterans legislation has not been introduced? If the minister had given us some indication of the legislation he intends to put before parliament I am quite sure he would realize he would not have been held up this long in getting his estimates passed, because the estimates were thoroughly gone over in the standing committee. We had no intention of holding up the estimates, and I do not accept the fact that we are holding them up now. What we are trying to do is to get some information on behalf of the veterans we represent.
The minister has been vague and evasive, and I refer to the remarks he made in the standing committee on veterans affairs. When I heard him at the time I did not realize he

was so evasive, but when asked about legislation being introduced this is what he said:
Well, as I indicated in the house, I would still hope to have this before the house during the coming month. This is not a definite commitment but I will do my best to try to get it into the house before the end of October. This is my objective. It may be that it might run into November, but it will be done in the not too distant future. It will be done before the end of the year.
As members can see, he was just going on and on, and that is why I say he was evasive. Because of the few weeks left between now and Christmas, I ask even if he does introduce legislation on behalf of the veterans, does he believe for one moment that any action can be taken on it this year? So far as his department and the veterans are concerned there will be no action this year on pension increases. No action will be taken on war veterans allowances or on any of the things veterans have been writing to us about, because it will be impossible for the house to deal with the legislation which the Prime Minister said he is going to put on the order paper between now and Christmas.
What does the minister intend to do about the committee's recommendations? Someone has said our recommendations contain 14 paragraphs, but the first one dealing with anything except platitudes is paragraph six, which I wish to read. But before doing so I remind members that the veterans affairs committee is made up of members from all parties, the majority of them from the government side. There was unanimous agreement on this recommendation which reads:
With respect to the subject matter of Bill C-13, it was unanimously agreed that more effective steps should be taken to observe November 11th as a national holiday and a solemn day of remembrance in all parts of Canada.
I do not believe the minister had any intention of taking notice of this recommendation. Some few weeks ago the hon. member for Kindersley rose on a question of privilege with regard to a labour bill which was before the house, and said he thought it deplorable Canada did not recognize Remembrance day as a national holiday. Just a few days ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre moved an amendment to that labour bill, calling for the recognition of Remembrance day as a holiday, but not one of the members on the government side voted for it. I remind hon. members again that the majority of members on the standing committee-

speechtext: When the committee rose on October 8 last clause 1 of the bill, with an amendment proposed thereto by the hon. member for Timiskaming and an amendment to the amendment by the hon. member for Lapointe, was being considered. The question is on the amendment to the amendment.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this measure has been useful in calling the attention of the public to some of the operations of this very large and very powerful corporation which controls virtually all the means of communication between the people of Ontario and Quebec. I am not sure whether it has called sufficient attention to some of their operations, indicating that the amendment presented here has some real substance, and the necessity of having some sort of watchdog over the operations of this company. I propose this afternoon to quote from two extremely interesting articles which appeared a couple of weeks ago in the Toronto Star, written by a Mr. Haggart, on the operations of the Bell Telephone Company and what he describes as its sibling company, the New York Telephone Company. These articles refer to the method by which this company disguises some of its charges to the public and the price people are asked

Private Bills
to pay for what is termed "local service and equipment". I recall that I paid my telephone bill today and this question occurred to my mind: just what is meant by "local service and equipment"? I know that it cost me quite a bit of money, but the telephone bill did not explain what I was paying for. Apparently in New York there is a public spirited gentleman called Levine who is making it his business to act as spokesman for the subscribers to the New York Telephone Company, exposing some of these charges that are made by the company without explanation. This article says:
Levine is the director and guiding spirit of an outfit called the American telephone consumer's council, which plans to join in court actions, appear before regulatory commissions, and generally raise hob with the phone company on behalf of its customers.
As most of us are customers, and few of us are shareholders, I am sure we will all cheer Mr. Levine on in his efforts:
In his current campaign against the cute concealment of extra charges on the phone bill under "local service and equipment", Levine is trying to whet the appetite of the consumer frauds branch of the New York attorney general's department.
Levine's petition laid out the complaint this way: "Undoubtedly, the New York Telephone Co. fears that if the charges were brought to the customer's attention by being itemized, the customer might cancel the luxury rentals.
"We demand an immediate investigation by the bureau of consumer frauds into this attempt by the New York Telephone Co. to mislead us as consumers"-
The charge in Toronto-
I should perhaps include this:
Levine's complaint about the concealment of monthly rental charges (he likes to call them "forever charges") -
I think that is a very nice term:
-is as true in Toronto as in New York.
The charge in Toronto for installing a princess phone-
And I am sure we would all love to have a princess phone:
-is $6.
Whether that is because you have some special connection with royalty, I do not know; or whether when you pick it up you get a princess at the other end, as when you pick up the telephone to send a telegram-

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: You are just dreaming.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Oh, I was afraid I would not get a princess for $6; but still I can hope. This article continues:

It also costs an extra 85 cents a month forever, and if the Princess is an extension the 85 cents is an addition to the extension charges of $1.25 a month.
A Princess extension, therefore, costs $31.20 the first year, and $25.20 for every year thereafter. In ten years, a Princess extension phone will cost the customer $258. New York dealers sell the same phone for $35 cash.

speechtext: I would be delighted to do so, Mr. Chairman. I am only surprised that I am required to do so; I thought it would have been self-evident. The object of this amendment is to place on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company individuals who will represent the people of Canada, the government of Canada and the customers of this company. I am merely advancing evidence to show how sorely needed are such inquisitors, such observers, in the operations of this company.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Would you like to hear something, sir, about coloured phones. The article continues in this way:
Regulatory commissions which are supposed to be the public watchdogs of monopoly public utilities seldom pay much attention to such charges, although they loom large both in the customer's phone bill and in the receipts of the phone companies. The single exception seems to be the state of New Jersey, where the public utilities commission recently ordered the charge for a coloured phone to be reduced to $4, and the monthly rental for an extension reduced to 90 cents. Across the river in New York, a coloured phone is $10; in Toronto it's $9. Any extension in Toronto, coloured or black, costs $1.25 a month, forever.
I suggest that this report indicates-and I presume it would not be published by the Star if it was not verified-the urgent need of some more permanent observation and surveillance of the operations of this company than can be provided by the board of transport commissioners. Hon. members will recall that in the original presentation of this bill it was stressed again and again that this is a purely Canadian company, a Canadian-owned company, with only a really minute smidgen of stock held by a nonCanadian. Of course, it is quite a small percentage; only some 2.6 per cent of the stock

is owned by a non-Canadian. But this happens to be the largest single block of stock owned by any shareholder.
Curiously enough it is owned by American Telephone & Telegraph Company, an organization which has its special contract agreement also with the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, which provides quite a little bit for the revenues of this company.
Among the interesting facts not disclosed in the propaganda pamphlet-and facts which the Bell company has no reason to be embarrassed about-is the involvement of American Telephone & Telegraph often called North America's largest company and the giant, paternal overseer of the Bell system.
The largest single shareholder in Bell of Canada is A.T. & T., with 2.6 per cent of the shares, or a total of 749,992.
This is two or three times as much Bell stock as anyone else owns.
The Bell pamphlet sent to subscribers this month does not even mention the existence of A.T.& T. Yet A.T.& T. was entitled to $1,600,000 in dividends out of Bell of Canada last year, and was paid another $4,700,000 under the terms of management contract and patent pool. (A.T. & T. takes 1 per cent off the top of Bell's gross telephone revenue.)
I suggest that this indicates the need for a very careful surveillance of the operations of this company, of the charges it is making and of the impact it has on the Canadian economy.
Specifically this bill asks us to authorize the appointment of five more directors. We were not able to get any very conclusive or definite statement out of the officers of the company when we met as to who such people would be. If one looks at the present board of directors the reason is obvious, of course. This article continues:
In fact, there is only one of these 11 directors who is not also a director of a bank. It's entirely likely that the bank just down your street is represented on the Bell board of directors-
Just as the Bell Company says that your neighbour down the street is probably a shareholder, that neighbour down the street in the form of a bank is probably represented on the board. According to this article the board of directors is composed of:
-the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank, the Toronto-Dominion Bank, La Banque Canadienne National each has one director on Bell; the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, has three. Montreal Trust and Royal Trust have two and three directors respectively on Bell. In addition, Sun Life, Crown Life, Norwich Union, Canada Life and Dominion Life are all represented on the Bell board of directors.
If I were one of those neighbours down the street with Bell Telephone stock myself, I'd want to ask questions about the huge amounts of new stock Bell sells to its employees at bargain-counter prices.

That is another method by which the illusion is created of a popularly owned and controlled organization in our midst.
It may be that eventually this house will pass this bill and the Bell Telephone Company will appoint five more directors. It may also be the case that again they will be chosen from the ranks of bank directors and directors of trust companies. But I would hope, sir, that we shall not leave the position of this company in its present state. I trust we shall not even be satisfied with appointing the sort of watchdogs of which I have been speaking, but that we have a thoroughgoing investigation into the operations of this company, an investigation which cannot be undertaken by the present regulatory body because it lacks the power to do so. If we are going to pass this bill I suggest that it is the duty of the government to bring in legislation which will increase and broaden the powers of the board of transport commissioners so that they can make a real investigation of the operations of this company, and enable the Canadian people to decide whether or not the time has come to remove from private hands altogether this octopus on which the whole of our economy in central Canada depends and from whose decisions the ordinary Canadian citizen literally has no recourse at all.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in discussing Bill No. S-27, let me say I am greatly surprised at the helplessness of the government. This bill has been coming back before the house every Thursday for several weeks, without the slightest amendment being brought to it, although that was what we requested of the mover of the bill himself.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder who is actually inciting the government not to take into account all the arguments we have submitted up to now.
Here, I wish to congratulate the hon. member who spoke previously for the fine statement he has just made. This is further proof that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) was right in submitting an amendment to the house to refute the words of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) who said, as reported on page 8638 of Hansard, that the mover of the amendment had good intentions. On the other hand, I doubt very much that either he or his supporters can seriously expect the Canadian parliament to pass this bill.
Mr. Chairman, I can assure you that on reading such a subsection, opposition mem-

Private Bills
bers ask themselves many questions, and the people generally have not finished asking some more. Through the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Lapointe, we are asking the government to make the Bell Telephone Company see to it that the five directors to be added to the board of directors are not shareholders, in order that various public bodies may have their say in such a powerful organization.
This trust is especially dangerous because it seems to find favour with this government as with the previous ones, probably because of its important contribution to the election funds of the old-line parties.
Mr. Chairman, we are in favour of private enterprise, but not in favour of almighty trusts which can give orders year after year to the government and this is why the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is constantly asking for rate increases. Today, under Bill S-27, it is asking to increase by five the number of its directors.
We are fully justified in wanting to know the reasons and in imposing conditions on the company, since it is authorized to tax the entire population at will. We are concerned, however, that old-line party members do not dare to reject those ever increasing demands of the company, probably because it is one of the reasons why trusts can overpower the voice of the people.
Its funds might have contributed to the election of governments up to now, which necessarily requires silence.
But whatever the reasons, it is the people who must pay. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the people now pay millions of dollars more for those small favours on election day. Those who were elected under this label must necessarily show their true colours by remaining the loyal servants of that company.
Am I right? Am I wrong? The facts are there to prove my statements.
Let us compare the rates charged the Bell Telephone Company of Canada's customers with those charged in other provinces. On the prairies the subscribers pay a rate of $3.90, and the rate is even lower in British Columbia, we pay more than $6.40 for the same service. And yet, in British Columbia, where there is a Social Credit government, companies' profits have increased by more than 100 per cent. Don't you think that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada can be an exception to that rule?
Therefore, I can see one reason only for increasing by five the number of the company's directors; it is to be able to deduct a 
few thousand dollars more from their income tax, depriving the government of revenues which it will have to take from the small wage earner who is unable to cheat because his income tax is deducted at the source.
I feel, then Mr. Chairman, that this is a fine opportunity for the government to take advantage of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada's request in order to require the company to choose the five new directors among the various social groups. Thus, the interests of the taxpayers will be protected.
If we grant full powers to this trust which is competition free-because, to my knowledge, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is not faced with too much competition-the government must take every precaution to prevent the people from being frustrated of their right to fair democratic treatment.
Somebody will object saying that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada is required to examine the balance sheet of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Indeed, it is that board which is responsible for representing the public in its relations with this company. But what can be done by that board, made up mostly of the mute members we find in this house, when they have been unable to stem the prohibitive prices we have now. Let us consider that, for calls from public booths, we have to pay 10 cents to unhook the receiver, instead of 5 cents as in the other provinces. That is a difference of 100 per cent, compared with other provinces, and it is the same for the whole schedule of telephone charges.
Some may say that it is because of the good service. They should ask people in the other provinces who are in a position to compare what the situation is. They will be the first ones to be disappointed by the inadequate service and the lack of control of charges to users. Indeed, if we do not check every day long-distance calls-and heaven knows how piany we have-we will have to pay for the bill of those who used our name.
One may say that when a report is made to the office, they correct the mistake quickly, but when it goes unnoticed, they also hurry to make us pay.
For all those reasons, Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), namely that five new directors should be appointed by municipalities, school boards, unions, chambers of commerce and employers and industrialists associations, to make sure that the majority of consumers will be represented in the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

Each of these new directors would be in a position to look into the administration of this company which, in fact, lives on the money paid to it by all the Canadian taxpayers.
If it is our duty to encourage private companies, it is also very urgent that we should protect the people against the danger of abuses from trusts that are too powerful for the government to lay down a policy for them.
The regulations must be complied with by the big fellows just like the small ones, and I am not aware that we have yet reached the stage of the law of the jungle.
That is why, to face up to some trusts, the government must assume its responsibilities and prescribe terms which, while enabling them to expand, will guarantee freedom in justice for all Canadian citizens.

Let us go on to the next objection that I see to the amendment. As I understand the rules of the house with regard to a bill of this sort, if the amendment were passed the Bell Telephone Company at that stage would be in the position of being able to withdraw the legislation and therefore nothing would be accomplished and additional directors would not be appointed. Therefore I think that the question whether the Bell Telephone Company should have five additional directors to be appointed by the company should be considered by the house on the merits of whether or not more directors are needed.
Mind you, because of the size of the Bell Telephone Company, with which I will deal in a moment or two, and because the house does not have the opportunity to deal with the affairs of this company very often, I agree that those occasions when they do come to

the house seeking amendments to their charter are legitimate occasions to review their operations in a reasonable manner. I do not believe in a prolonged filibuster on the subject but I believe there should be a reasonable review. On these occasions members of the house, the elected representatives of the people, should be able to express their views and concerns with reference to the magnitude of the Bell Telephone Company and some of its practices. I think this would be very worth while. I hope the company will take note of the fact that members from all parts of the house have spoken on this bill and that this must reflect a certain concern throughout the country with regard to some of their operations. I am thinking specifically about their ownership of Northern Electric and the competition of that company with other private companies in the same field.
There is another matter on which I should like to say a word or two. I think most of the members of the house are believers in free enterprise. Sometimes the press indicates that one who criticizes such a utility or company may not support free enterprise, but I hasten to say that ever since I can remember it has been my impression that the essence of free enterprise is competition. Competition in any field makes for free enterprise that is healthy and guarantees the people of the country good service.
I remember when I had an opportunity to visit Moscow at the time of the world's ice hockey championships in 1957 I found the service in the restaurant in the hotel to be absolutely terrible. I waited for three quarters of an hour to be served because there was not another restaurant across the street to which I could go. I think this is an example of something that happens when there is no competition, and of the fact that competition is of the essence of free enterprise.
Unfortunately some enterprises must be run as monopolies. The Bell Telephone Company has become a very large monopoly. I think all members will agree that you cannot have half a dozen telephone companies stringing wires along the streets. You would be in a position of attempting to call someone and finding he was served by another company, and you would have a very complicated process to go through in order to reach him. As a consequence, a telephone company is one operation which, to be effectively run, has to be run as a monopoly. Under such circumstances there is a necessity for the government to intervene, to some extent, in the operation of the business because free 20220-591i
