enterprise as such does not exist wherever there is a monopoly of this type.
A long time ago, it was established that the board of transport commissioners would be the body which would oversee the operations of the telephone company. They have certain terms of reference for doing that job. Now I suggest, and I think a good case could be made out, that the present powers of the board of transport commissioners are not sufficiently strong to enable them to do as efficient a job of overseeing this particular monopoly. I suggest that rather than introduce amendments which would add one or more directors appointed by the government or by parliament to the Bell Telephone Company, the proper way to deal with the question is to beef up the board of transport commissioners. If the personnel of the board are not strong enough, if more personnel is needed to do the amount of work necessary or if the powers of the board are insufficient to do the job, and I do not know this because I have not had experience with it, then let us act in that direction. I would certainly conclude from the experience I have had that the board of transport commissioners does not have sufficient power to oversee the operations of the Bell Telephone, particularly in relationship to the ownership of Northern Electric by that company. The remedy therefore lies in legislation to change the position of the board of transport commissioners and give them the power to carry out this function.
I spoke earlier for a moment, Mr. Chairman, about the ownership of Northern Electric by the Bell Telephone Company. We want to remember that we are not talking simply about a telephone company, we are talking about an empire. We are talking about an organization that had a gross income of $471 million for a year. This company has become so big that it is bigger than many governments that exist in the world today. It is a company which, even with a very strong board of transport commissioners or some other public utilities body, will need to be watched carefully at all times. In so far as the ownership of Northern Electric is concerned, other members have reviewed the fact that Bell owns all the shares of Northern Electric by virtue of the interpretation of a clause giving the company power to hold shares of or make arrangements with other companies involved in telephone business. The fact that Northern Electric owns a telephone line which stretches a short distance in the city of Montreal has been used

as the back door for Bell Telephone to acquire ownership of this giant Northern Electric, which provides Bell Telephone with all its wire, cable and other such supplies.
I do not necessarily argue over the question that the Bell Telephone Company is manufacturing wire and cable for its own use. Let us remember also that Northern Electric are not content with supplying the big market offered by the Bell Telephone monopoly, but all Bell's customers have no opportunity to go anywhere else. Bell then uses its subsidiary, Northern Electric, to supply its requirements for this vast market and then Northern turns around and competes in the ordinary market with the smaller companies that exist in Canada which are manufacturing wire, cable and so on. I suggest that they have little chance of being able to compete with Northern in those circumstances.
I questioned the officials of the Bell Telephone Company on this matter during the hearings before the committee. They were quick to make the point that Bell Telephone bought all their supplies from Northern Electric at a rate that was much lower than the market cost, and therefore the public interest was being served. However, Mr. Chairman, the representatives of the other companies in Canada quickly made the point that this was not true. They said that, certainly, the rate that was being paid for these goods would appear to be lower than the market price, but when you consider the quantity discount other companies might offer, this may not be the case. They never had the opportunity of competing for these supplies to Bell Telephone. They say, give us a chance to compete for Bell's supplies along with Northern Electric and we will quote a price on these goods that will be lower than that which the Bell Telephone Company is presently paying Northern Electric. These companies make what appears to me to be a very valid point. Therefore Bell is paying an artificially high rate for these supplies to Northern Electric. Since the rate for telephones is set on the basis of allowing the company a reasonable profit after costs this means, in effect, that the telephone subscribers of this country are, to a substantial extent, helping Northern Electric provide unfair competition to companies that are operating the same type of business as Northern Electric in this country today. It is to this aspect of the matter that I object.

I feel that any court examination, and there has not been any, of the power of the Bell Telephone to own Northern Electric would result in a finding that such ownership was ultra vires of the powers of Bell Telephone.
I would strongly urge, Mr. Chairman, that the only way this matter can get before the Supreme Court of Canada is by a reference.
I feel it is in the public interest that the government should refer to the supreme court the question of whether or not the ownership of Northern Electric is proper, when it depends upon the ownership by Northern of this one wire. If Bell Telephone wanted to retain Northern Electric to do their manufacturing of their supplies, they could quite legally do that and not enter the competitive field with other companies manufacturing the same line of goods. Mr. Chairman, prior to the private members' hour I was making reference to recommendations that the committee on veterans affairs had made to the minister of the department. I had almost completed my remarks in regard to the first recommendation; that is, in regard to Remembrance day. I would say to the minister at this time *that I regret finding myself in the position where I must state my mind, on behalf of the people whom I represent and particularly on behalf of the veterans whom I represent, *in regard to the inaction, I might say, of the minister of this department. In saying that I would also like to remind the minister Ahat if he would put himself in my position, .being a member of that standing committee and having the feeling that the recommen-. dations on which we spent so many hours are going to be disregarded altogether by him and his department, he would understand my resentment, if he wishes to take it that way.
I now come to the second recommendation made by the committee, which was in regard to amendments to the Pension Act. I am of the opinion that several sections of that act should be reviewed with a view to changing them. I admit that perhaps up to the present time they have been necessary, and were necessary particularly in the years immediately after world war II. I refer to section 5 (5) in which full power with regard to the interpretation of the act is given to the commission. This is an extraordinary type of act in Canadian justice. I believe there are very few other acts that have been passed by this parliament and our predecessors that are not subject to interpretation and decision


by the courts. This act happens to be one exception. As many hon. members have informed the minister in this debate on his estimates, we believe it is now time this act was reviewed. I refer to one hon. member who spoke in the house yesterday afternoon and who is in fact a non-veteran; therefore I compliment him for saying this. I have reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who said:
What we are really seeking is not a basic change in much of that legislation, but rather the kind of improvement which will meet the situation existing today.
I think that is all the members of the veterans affairs committee were trying to do when we asked the minister to review section 70, which is commonly known as the benefit of the doubt section. Any review of Hansard will show that from time to time members of parliament have tried to change the interpretation which the Canadian pension commission has been putting on this particular section. Another section we have been trying to change is 13 (2). In this regard I would point out that there has been one change that I know of in regard to the phrase "arising out of and directly connected with". The word "and" in that section has been changed to "or", and it now reads, "arising out of or directly connected with".
I maintain that this is significant, in that prior to the change from "and" to "or" the pension commission felt they had to be satisfied that the applicant qualified in regard to both those terms. It was the intent of parliament that he only had to qualify under one. We maintain that the members of the pension commission do not recognize this, or so it seems to us who are fighting these cases. I do not say this just as a member of the opposition, because hon. members opposite have made reference to this particular section, as well as to section 70. In this connection I would refer to the problem the British government had in regard to this particular type of act. I could say some very harsh words about the Canadian pension commission, and perhaps I have already said some very harsh words about that body; but I hope those on that commission as well as the officials of the department realize that I must attack all officials rather than perhaps one or two who are responsible for the block, if I may call it that, which apparently exists between what members of parliament are trying to do-the intent of parliament, if you want to put it that way-and the way in

which they are actually administering the act.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said, we believe we must keep up to date; and if the minister has not brought in or is not going to bring in any changes to this act,
I think it is high time he considered changing some of its sections. I repeat again, Mr. Chairman, that section 5 (5) should be reviewed, section 13 (2) should be reviewed, section 63 (5) should be reviewed and section 70 should be reviewed.
I mentioned that I would say something about what happened in the United Kingdom. During the committee discussion on section 70 and section 13 (2) I had something to say because at that time I believe I had a bill dealing with this very matter referred to the committee on veterans affairs for investigation. At that time the most convincing argument that I think was put forward was in connection with the maiden speech of Lord Denning in the United Kingdom House of Lords. I should like to put part of that speech on the record, not only for the minister's benefit but for the benefit of the veterans who will read the contents of Hansard. Lord Denning said at that time:
My Lords, it has been my lot as a judge to review the decisions of many tribunals, and may I say how welcome it is that this important report should be accepted by all parties in the state, because it contains and reaffirms a constitutional principle of the first importance-namely that these tribunals are not part of the administrative machinery of government under the control of departments; they are part of the judicial system of the land under the rule of law. This report shows how that principle should be put into practice. These tribunals should, whenever appropriate, give reasons for their decisions, and their decisions should be subject to appeal to the courts on points of law.
This is what I have always maintained, that the commission is not capable of determining points of law. It so happens that in my opinion a precedent is set by some decision of a member of the commission and that precedent is followed throughout in practically every case.
Then later on His Lordship said:
I will tell Your Lordships something about an appeal structure with which I had some connection-namely the pensions appeals tribunal. After the war the late Lord Jowitt, of honoured memory, appointed me as the nominated judge to hear all appeals from ex-servicemen. The machinery of appeal is this. The ministry look into a case, and say whether or not it is a proper case for a pension. If they reject it, there is an appeal to the high court on points of law. I was nominated as the judge to hear all these appeals.
See how the course of justice may unknowingly go wrong. I had not been sitting for two or three weeks, when I realized that the tribunals had been
Supply-Veterans Affairs putting the burden of proof the wrong way-they were putting it on the service man to prove his disability was attributable to war service.
The hon. member for Charlotte mentioned this afternoon that the benefit of the doubt was put the wrong way by the commission. Parliament in Canada has been contending for a number of years that this is wrong, but no action has been taken by the minister's department to change the section of the act and to spell this out to the commission. It seems to me that the commissioners themselves pay no attention to what is the intent of parliament. We have tried in every possible manner. I would say, to impress upon these people that this is what we mean; but apparently there is someone on the commission who, in my opinion, has said that we do not know what we are talking about and that the present way is the way it is going to be.
Lord Denning went on to say this:
That had been the law before 1943; but in 1943 the royal warrant was amended to say that if a man was fit when he went into the service and disabled when he came out, there should be a presumption, and a compelling presumption, that his disablement was due to war service and that the burden was on the ministry, if they could, to prove the contrary. So far as I could see, despite the change in the royal warrant, the tribunals had gone on in the old way. They were saying in their reasons, "We cannot find sufficient ground for saying that this was attributable to war service".
I hope I was right, but in every case I allowed the appeal.
Further than that, there arose the question of those people whose cases had been decided in the last two years on a wrong basis.
I would say that we have many such cases in Canada which have been decided on a wrong basis.
Application was made to extend the time limit for an appeal. The attorney general of the day argued that a judge had no power to give an extension of time. I held that am extension of time was permissible, and made it reasonably clear that in every case the time would be extended; whereupon the government of the day, very properly, set up a special review tribunal which reviewed all those cases. As a result, many men got the pensions to which they were entitled, and counsel for the British Legion, addressing me afterwards, told me how admirably the review tribunal had done their work.
I say it is time that we in Canada recognized what has happened in the United Kingdom and amended our act accordingly.
His Lordship goes on:
What I have said shows how, quite unconsciously and unmeaningly, a tribunal may slip into error and may need to be corrected. But that is not the only purpose of an appeal. Another purpose is to get uniform decisions. There were 14 or 15 tribunals operating all over the country, and one might come to a decision different from that of another. There

Supply-Veterans Affairs
were difficult cases. Cancer, for example, is a very difficult and arguable case. On the one hand, doctors could not say what was the cause of cancer, so how could it be said that it was not due to war service? On the other hand, it was said that cancer is just as prevalent in civilian life as it is in the army, and that there is no possibility of its being due to war service. One tribunal would decide a case in one way and another tribunal would decide in quite a different way. How unfortunate for all the widows and other dependants. We arranged to have test cases in which the medical evidence and the legal position in a typical case of cancer could be settled and decided, so that that might act as a signpost for all other cases of that type. That was done in regard to cancer, leukaemia, varicose veins and other ailments which continually arose, so we achieved uniformity of decision. That, then, is the other value of an appeal.
I might say here that I personally in the past year have had a couple of cases of exservicemen who had developed multiple sclerosis, and in neither one was I successful in getting a settlement for the applicant, although I knew full well that others of my colleagues had had more success in getting these cases through the Canadian pension commission. I wonder why I was not successful. I think my cases were just as valid as any of the others. In fact the records of one case showed that the first symptoms of multiple sclerosis appeared while this serviceman was in the service, and as a result he was discharged. I understand from the medical profession that no one knows how multiple sclerosis starts. Therefore how can it be determined whether or not it was attributable to war service in this case? Similarly with cancer, and I think His Lordship said something about that in the course of his remarks. In some cases of cancer it has been found in later years that owing to a bump received a cyst or growth formed and turned out to be malignant. No one knows how cancer starts. No one knows how multiple sclerosis starts. Therefore how can the Canadian pension commission in their wisdom say that this sort of thing is not attributable to war service? That is my point. However, if a ruling were made that all multiple sclerosis cases were not to be considered for pension, perhaps I would accept it; but when the commission accepts one case and not another I wonder why.
His Lordship goes on to say:
As a result of this experience, I would ask that, if appeals are to be limited to points of law, a liberal interpretation should be given as to what constitutes a point of law. I would give Your Lordships one illustration. Gunner Lee had suffered a great deal from stomach trouble while in the army. He had reported to army doctors, and they had pooh-poohed him and put the case on one side. One suggested that he was malingering. When


he went to a civilian hospital it was found that his condition was by then inoperable and he died. His widow brought the case which eventually came to me. She conducted it in person. The man's captain, his comrades and his wife herself proved how he had reported sick to the army doctors and not been given attention; and the tribunal had decided against him simply because nothing appeared in his medical history sheet in regard to his complaints. Medical history sheets, however, may be incomplete. Rightly or wrongly, I held that if a tribunal comes to an unreasonable conclusion, that is a point of law with which courts can interfere. I am glad to say that only a year ago this house, in its judicial capacity, held that if a tribunal comes to a conclusion to which no reasonable man could come, that is a point of law on which the courts can interfere. In passing, may I express the hope that in any structure which is made in future the jurisdiction of this house in its judicial capacity will be preserved. Those who remember the workmen's compensation cases which came to this house will recall the liberal interpretation then given by the house in its judicial capacity-that the burden should not be on the workman who is injured but on his employer.
I could present many cases in respect of this benefit of the doubt clause, although I do not think that is necessary. Perhaps I should just ask the minister to read the remarks of hon. members who have spoken during our consideration of his estimates yesterday and today, counting the number of times the benefit of the doubt clause has been mentioned. I do not refer to the comments of members of the opposition only, but also to those remarks made by members of his own party. Perhaps the minister will consider the many briefs he has received from the various veterans organizations in Canada and count the number of references in those briefs to this same clause.
In view of the number of times the benefit of the doubt aspect of veterans problems has been referred to one must come to the conclusion that there is something wrong in its interpretation. I feel that parliament has done almost everything possible to bring this situation to the attention of the minister and his department. I do not believe the commissioners are carrying out the intent of parliament. Perhaps we should take some action to change the type of commission we now have. Mr. Chairman, I have said some very harsh things about the pension commission, and I must warn the house that unless some change takes place in the interpretation of this clause by that commission, as long as I am a member of this house I will have to use similar terms.
In view of the experience we have gained over the past number of years in respect of veterans pensions, I think it is time we paid attention to what Lord Denning of the United

Kingdom, said in this regard. It is time this legislation was changed. We have tried to make a change but apparently the commission has seen fit not to accept or follow our suggestions.
Several other things mentioned by members of the veterans affairs committee are worthy of repetition. First, I should like to refer to that committee's recommendation in respect of Remembrance day. What happened to that recommendation? Second, I should like to refer again to the benefit of the doubt clause and the committee's recommendation in relation to it. I think enough has been said about that particular aspect of veterans affairs problems.
Paragraph 13 of the recommendations of the committee on veterans affairs is related to increases in pensions. The minister implied, or at least I am under this impression, that there may be something done in this regard in the near future. I had hoped the minister would be more specific in his statement, because he must have received many letters of the type we have received from veterans, complaining that their pensions as of two years ago are no longer adequate in view of the increased cost of living and the decreased purchasing value of the dollar. I feel there should be automatic adjustments in those pensions. This point has been raised by several members during our consideration of the minister's estimates. Perhaps every three years the officials of the minister's department should appraise the cost of living and adjust these pensions accordingly. It should not be necessary for members of parliament to take up the time of this house in an attempt to impress upon the minister that because of increasing costs pensions should be adjusted. Surely that was the intent of the Canadian people when, through their elected representatives, they offered these pensions to veterans, whether they be disability pensions or veterans allowances. The people of Canada have felt that Canadian veterans should be taken care of, and I think it is the minister's duty to see that that wish is carried out.
Mr. Chairman, as a member of parliament it is my duty to impress upon the minister of this department the merits of the many suggestions made by myself and by other members. I should like to say a word or two in respect of the clause in the War Veterans Allowances Act which refers to the 365 day duty period in the United Kingdom. I did sponsor a bill which embodied certain changes in that clause, but unfortunately that 20220-592
Supply-Veterans Affairs bill was talked out. Many members of this house will agree that the intention behind the bill was to eliminate discrimination by the Canadian government in respect of veterans receiving these allowances. Apparently we are not looking after our own veterans so far as pensions are concerned because of the application of the 365 day limit. At the same time we are recognizing individuals as veterans eligible for allowances who were veterans in allied forces. Any individual who was a member of the armed forces of any allied country such as Russia, Italy, Belgium, France and many others, who lived in Canada for a period of ten years, can qualify under the War Veterans Allowances Act. On the other hand, if one of our own Canadian veterans served in the United Kingdom for a period of only 364 days he cannot qualify. That is discrimination and I hope the minister will give some consideration to this situation.
As a result of reports I have received I understand that an announcement was made on the C.B.C. yesterday morning to the effect that the Sunnybrook hospital in Toronto is under new management. I have heard rumours to the effect that the Ste. Foy hospital in Quebec city is either now under new management or will be under new management very shortly. In fairness to members of parliament, announcements of this kind should be made in parliament rather than through the news media, availing members of parliament an opportunity of informing their constituents of these changes.
The minister made a commitment to the standing committee on veterans affairs that before changes, of the nature to which I have referred, took place there would be consultations with veterans organizations concerned with the changes. Whether that took place or not I am not in a position to know, because the first word I heard in this regard was in the form of a report about that C.B.C. broadcast.
The minister also said in his opening remarks that he would answer any reasonable question asked. I have one question to ask him. Will the minister tell the house what legislation he proposes to bring into this house before the end of this session in respect of veterans affairs?

ities for domiciliary care. I think that is of great importance. I was very interested this afternoon in some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Edmonton West with respect to the projections in regard to our disability pensioners, war veterans allowance recipients, veterans requiring treatment, and one other subject I will deal with in a moment. We do have some projections at the moment, and with regard to the figures he used this afternoon the experience of 20 years with first world war veterans involving a rising curve for about 20 years and then going down appears to be repeating itself with world war II veterans.
It seems to us that in the case of disability pensioners we have perhaps reached a plateau, with the tendency now being for the curve to go down, which is in effect a repetition of the previous experience. In the case of war veterans allowance recipients, if we use past experience to project a curve into the future it will probably be about 1985 when the top of the curve is reached when it will likely be at a considerably higher figure than anything projected in earlier years, in terms of numbers.
I think I must agree there, as well, that there are so many uncertain factors in this that the curve could be different from one which is constructed on past experience. There is a question, as the hon. member has suggested, of social security measures, better hospital facilities and perhaps a different attitude on the part of some men who may want to be looked after within their own communities. There are so many imponderables there, it is really difficult to project a curve.
In the case of treatment services, of course to some extent the same considerations apply. Our curve of active treatment patients is of course a downward one, while the chronic and domiciliary care of patients is still on the increase and is likely to continue. By the way, I do regret the delay in the printing of the annual report. I am now informed it was signed and presented to the printers in the normal fashion, in the normal time, but apparently there has been some difficulty which is attributed-this is hearsay-to the fact that this house has not recessed as it formerly did at this time of year. I am told it will be possible perhaps to have a projection for five or ten years for disability pensioners. In so far as such a curve can be established, and there are qualifications to it, perhaps we may be able to present it in the way we do the annual report. Certainly I

Supply-Veterans Affairs hope we may be able to supply this information for the use of hon. members who may desire it.
There is one last point, Mr. Chairman, and I am extremely interested in it. I refer to veterans, not in the legal sense we use that term, as referring to ex-combatants, but to people leaving the services as well as those who are taking part in the peace keeping operations on behalf of Canada. I refer to such circumstances as we now have in Cyprus. I think I must agree that a new concept has to be evolved here. I think we have to treat these people differently, perhaps, than we did the veterans of world wars I and II and the Korean war. The concept of that time, if I can recall the situation correctly, related to the question of rehabilitation of people perhaps in an economy that everyone really thought might present difficulties. There were large numbers of people, and the circumstances of their service certainly were very different, in terms of benefits, from the circumstances of today. I must agree that a new look must be taken at this situation. As the hon. member mentioned this afternoon, he and I have had at least one conversation about this matter. I have had some conversations with other members and with some officials in my own department, with a view to trying to assess this situation and assess what kind of policy may emerge from the situation. We hope that something useful will emerge. I believe we are moving into an era in which we have to think of these people in a different way than we have. We have been thinking about rehabilitation as it related to the masses who went forward under the banners of the army, navy and air force to do their part under extremely difficult circumstances, when there were many casualties, a great deal of suffering and a great requirement for rehabilitation afterwards. I think this is something which should be undertaken, and I must agree with that.
There have been a number of other points raised, Mr. Chairman, but I believe I have largely answered the main comments that have been made here. I do want to assure the members of the standing committee that their recommendations are taken very seriously and given serious consideration. As time develops I think you will find that most of them will have been accepted. As I said this afternoon, I agree that hon. members are entitled to have the recommendations accepted or reasons given for the refusal to

I am sure the officials of the department and myself will take careful note of the things that have been said this afternoon and yesterday in attempting to meet the wishes of parliament with regard to veterans legislation.

They deal with such things as books of remembrance, battlefields memorials, and over the page you find maintenance of departmental cemeteries and plots, and commonwealth war graves commission. I think it is the function of the Department of Veterans Affairs to acquaint the people of Canada with the work of the commonwealth war graves commission and some of the other things I have mentioned, so that the people will realize the sacrifice that was involved in the various wars.
The extent of the work of the commonwealth war graves commission is not generally known. I asked the officials of the department, when they published the report of 1961 and the one in the following year, to pay some attention to that matter and list the number of areas in which our Canadian dead of both world wars are buried. It is a very large figure; 137 cemeteries scattered around the world, but chiefly in northwest Europe. There are three outstanding memorials of world war I and three of world war II in countries overseas, where the names of the missing have been engraved. Canada's prestige in countries that were liberated in world wars I and II stands very high, and the memorials are there for the people of those coun-

tries to see, in France, Belgium and Holland in particular. The people of those countries participate in ceremonies each year at some of the cemeteries in which Canadians are buried and at the memorials where the names of the missing are engraved.
Unfortunately the Canadian people seldom, unless they travel overseas, see these memorials or the cemeteries. It is a very depressing visit to motor through that strip of Belgium and Holland where so many people died and were buried in both world wars, and I think it should not be carried too far. On the other hand, I think it is important that the war graves commission should continue its work; it is important that these memorials should be maintained and it is important that some of these battlefields should be kept in a state whereby they are available for visiting Canadians. The Department of Veterans Affairs, with the co-operation of the national film board, had produced a film called "The Fields of Sacrifice" in order to bring to the Canadian people pictures of these memorials, some of the cemeteries and the areas in which Canadians fought and died, so their relatives who cannot travel overseas will at least have some idea of where their loved ones served. I hoped the minister would say something about that film. It is not a possession of the Department of Veterans Affairs but the idea originated with that department. I would like to know-and the minister can answer later-how many of those films have been made available and have been taken up by Legion branches and educational institutions across this country. It is now October 22. The film was designed to prepare the way for Remembrance day, which should be a day of dedication and memory for Canadian citizens. I would like to know how useful this film has been. Last year there were displays in some of the theatres in Ottawa and some of the major cities across the country. In the 16 millimetre version this film was to be made available in very large numbers. I would like to know what the facts are in this regard.
I would also like to know what the department is doing with regard to a project which was started when I had some responsibility for the Department of Veterans Affairs. This was a project with regard to the Vimy Ridge battlefield in France, an area of 250 acres given by France to Canada; it is Canadian soil. I suggest that plans be made to put that battlefield area in somewhat better condition, and that this should be done after the fashion
Supply

Veterans Affairs of the field of Gettysburg in the United States, which has been restored to the appearance it had 100 years ago and which is visited by about 1J million tourists every year. In 1967 we will have the anniversary of the battle of Vimy Ridge; that year is the year in which we will be celebrating confederation.
I took some tentative steps toward having work done at Vimy Ridge, looking forward to 1967. I hope the minister can give us a report on that project.
The last I heard about it, we had photographs taken over there by the Canadian army, with the co-operation of the air force, a model was constructed here in Ottawa and various plans were undertaken to improve the roads there. I suggested that the commonwealth war graves commission be asked to improve the general area, which has been covered with a forest of trees and does not resemble the area as it was 50 years ago.
I suggested that a great many of those trees should be cut down and that steps should be taken to beautify more than has been done up to the present, although a great deal has been done, the general area around the Vimy memorial itself, the approaches to it, and so on. I suggested that the seven craters, which are the only surviving craters of the first world war as far as I know, should all be marked, because they had names at the time of the battle of Vimy Ridge.
The front line trench system of years ago was cemented in and is a great attraction to tourists. I suggested that one of the communications trenches be restored as a reminder of the conditions under which people fought in that war. I would like to know what, if anything, has been done in this regard. At the battle area of Beaumont-Hamel a very excellent undertaking was completed, or virtually completed, one or two years ago. There at Beaumont-Hamel you can see the area over which the Royal Newfoundland regiment advanced from their front line trenches, the gaps in the wire through which they attempted to move and where they were mown down. I think that about 90 per cent of the regiment were either killed or wounded. These places are far away. Nevertheless 100,000 Canadians visit Europe each year and if they were aware of these memorials I think being tourists and being proud to be Canadians, they would visit them. There is Beaumont-Hamel, Vimy Ridge, the Menin gate, the monument at Saint-Julien recalling the first gas attack in the history of the world where the Canadians gained great distinction; these places have a special significance for Canada

Supply-Veterans Affairs and should be more thoroughly known. Then of course there are memorials and cemeteries in other parts of the world. I should like the minister to tell us something about this matter.
I should like to take another minute or two to go to another subject. There is no government department keenly interested in a military museum. We have, of course, a military museum in Ottawa which I described years ago as the smallest museum in the world, and plans are under way to erect other buildings which will give Canadians some idea of their past history. I should like to know from the minister whether representatives of the Department of Veterans Affairs are sitting in with the planners of the other museums which are going to be constructed in Ottawa over the years, and are they going to see that the military history of Canada is adequately presented? Somebody has to take an interest in this. It cannot be left to the Department of National Defence, although their historical section will give co-operation. I think the Department of Veterans Affairs is the one to take the lead in influencing those who will have some responsibility for the portraying of Canada's military history. We have a military history going back for over 300 years. It is a fascinating history. But it has been played down to a great extent in Canada and I think it should be emphasized. Other countries take note of their military history; they have military museums as well as the preservation of battlefield areas. I hope the minister can tell us something about this also.
One other project I had hoped to advance which I think would be a good confederation celebration project is the publication of the military history of Canada from the earliest times to the present. I do not know whether the two years remaining are sufficient for this to be done, but here again the Department of Veterans Affairs, in addition to its duties about which we have been talking tonight, could play a leading part on behalf of Canadian veterans and their relatives. It is a great story. It is the story of Canada's military history, and I hazard the guess that if someone would undertake to write the story of the land settlement of Canada it would be a story of settlement of this country very largely by veterans. In the Atlantic provinces, the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and particularly British Columbia the opening up of the country and the settlement of the land was done I think very 

largely by veterans. There is a story which should be told and which should be incorporated in our history books. Out in the prairie provinces once again you will find that a great deal of the opening up of that territory was done by veterans. Land grants were made. People on discharge made their contribution in days of peace toward opening up this country.
I have drawn the committee's attention to these matters, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to prolong the discussion but I should like to have a comment from the minister if he has information on these subjects.

I think this might be a good occasion to pay tribute to the Royal Canadian Legion on the organization of their maple leaf tour this summer which gave us the opportunity to take part in a pilgrimage to the battlefields and last resting places of our comrades. Mention was made of the Vimy memorial. This is probably one of the greatest memorials in Europe. There is some damage to the memorial and research is being done on how to correct it. It is suspected at the moment that the damage has been caused by chemicals drifting through the air toward the monument. It is a most impressive sight and I want to add my words of tribute to Mr. Paul Piroson who has done such a magnificent job and who will be retiring shortly. There is a great deal of work to be done at Vimy. As was mentioned, a plan was developed a little while ago which involves arranging for the relocation of a road, some fencing and I think some general landscaping. In that regard I think we will need an expert to give advice on how that should be done. There is so much that needs to be done there.
Again, one could spend a great deal of time in talking about the memorial and the communication trenches. Some of these have been completed within the last two or three years but the galleries, the underground areas, are not fully reconstructed. The damage of the war of 1939-45 has not been completely corrected and a lot of work needs to be done. There is a story to be told about Vimy and anyone with any degree of eloquence could spend hours talking about the underground passages. We know so little about these things in Canada and I heartily agree we must make every effort to make sure that the Canadian people know what is there. We must organize things in such a way that Vimy will serve as a place of honour, a show window for Canada. I could not agree more and I can only say that I pledge myself to undertake to the best of my ability, with the full co-operation of the department, I am sure, to continue this work to make of Vimy that which we all hope it will be. Whether we can complete the whole project by 1967 is a little difficult to say. I do not know whether such a target can be reached but at least the work certainly will go forward.

Mr. Chairman, as minister responsible for the emergency measures organization I would recall to hon. members that evidence was given to the special parliamentary committee on defence both by myself and the staff of the emergency measures organization on July 18 and again on July 23 at which times the program of the emergency measures organization was outlined and an indication was given of the intentions with regard to emergency measures and also as to the priorities which would be observed in the implementation of this program.
The objectives of the civil emergency planning program remain the same as disclosed to the committee, namely to make preparations to help ensure maximum survival of the Canadian population and resources in a nuclear or conventional war, and to assist the provincial governments and through them the municipalities in coping not only with a war emergency but also with peacetime disasters whenever requested to do so and when the damage is beyond the capabilities of these local governments. We would like to encourage local civil defence organizations to publicize their preparedness and availability for any type of disaster. We hope that nuclear war will never occur, but there is no guarantee that the present international climate will not degenerate into cold war or actual conflict. Also we know that peacetime disasters do occur periodically and in either context civil emergency planning is a good
Supply-Defence Production insurance policy. We believe that as long as military defence is required so too will civil defence be required.
Civil defence planning is still being actively pursued in the United Kingdom and the United States and other NATO countries, and there is continued close consultation between the NATO countries, including Canada, on this matter.
I believe that adequate progress is being made in civil emergency planning in Canada. Vote 20 covers the administrative costs of the emergency measures organization, including the civil defence college at Arnprior. The total staff remains modest in size, numbering approximately 90, including the staff of the 10 regional offices, and 96 at the civil defence college. Vote 25 includes the program for the provision of radiac instruments to provinces on a cost sharing basis, the provinces reimbursing 25 per cent of the cost. These instruments would be used for the detection and measuring of radioactive fallout. Again good progress has been made, with six provinces having agreed to participate in the new program.
Vote 30, which provides for financial assistance programs to the provinces and from them to the municipalities, indicates a slight increase over last year. I believe that the provinces are progressing satisfactorily in this field. I may say we are pleased to note that there is a greater tendency in the provinces to group municipalities into larger county organizations, which the federal emergency organization encourages as it provides for a more efficient and economic organization.
To ensure the continued adequacy and effectiveness of civil defence preparations, the emergency measures organization and national defence have reviewed the effective decision to increase the emphasis on purely military training in relation to the militia. It will be recalled that the regular army will have as its second role responsibility for preparing for civil defence operation. As stated in the terms of reference of the Suttie committee, and I quote:
It must be recognized that in the event of an all-out nuclear war, all military forces would be employed on survival operations. Therefore, the militia, with all available regulars, would be required to provide a framework for the conduct of survival operations, using a large number of civilians.
The terms of reference also state that the militia will assist in fulfilling the army's national survival responsibilities. On the basis of the latest assumptions and require-

Supply-Defence Production ments, national defence will continue to maintain or improve:
(i)	the warning system against possible enemy attacks;
(ii)	the system for the location of nuclear detonations in likely target areas and the forecasting and determining of fallout and warning to the public;
(iii)	its plans for re-entry operations into damaged areas or areas of serious fallout;
(iv)	the emergency government communications network, which is part of the peacetime Canadian army signal system. A survey will be carried out in the near future, under the direction of the emergency measures organization, to prepare plans for the provision of regional emergency government headquarters in the four provinces where these are not already available, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. The completion of these headquarters will then permit the installation of the communications equipment, most of which has already been acquired.
The Canadian army, through its command and area headquarters, will maintain emergency readiness plans up to date, so that all units of the regular army and militia would be capable of carrying out survival operations on short notice. It is intended to include the necessary funds to continue the implementation of such a program in the national defence five year budgetary estimates.
The fourth report of the special committee on defence, I am pleased to see, contains chapter 3 which has been devoted entirely to civil emergency planning. We have noted the recommendations of the committee. I should like to review briefly these recommendations. I would agree generally with the three aims stated for the emergency measures organization by the committee in paragraph 30, that is, to help insure continuity of civilian government, the identification and allocation of resources after an attack, and that the civilian population be informed and able to make use of any existing protective facilities.
I concur with the statement in paragraph 31 to the effect that a fundamental task is to ensure the availability of an effective communications system across the country in the event of an emergency. To ensure such communications in protected facilities in all provinces, we are considering the completion of the regional headquarters network in the remaining four provinces of New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. Also discussions are being con-

tinued with all communications companies to ensure maximum utilization of all networks in an emergency.
Although, as stated in paragraph 32 of the report, it would be desirable to have a civil defence organization in all municipalities, I am not satisfied that we should consider it a priority. The important aspect at this time is to provide a capability in and around larger populated areas, making maximum use of the funds available through the financial assistance program. Such larger municipalities could provide assistance to smaller ones as required, whether in peacetime or wartime disasters. Also, it is our belief that planning is more effective and economical if smaller municipalities are grouped into county organizations.
As stated in paragraph 33 of the report, and I quote:
It is important that the responsibilities and the authorities at each level of government be defined under these varying conditions.
With regard to peacetime disasters, and in respect of this definition of responsibility, a very careful study was initiated some time ago and we are now consulting informally with the provinces and comparing notes with the United States. Specific recommendations can be expected to emerge from these discussions.
With regard to wartime responsibilities, the emergency measures organization has had under discussion with all departments and all provinces for some time, a specific outline of division of responsibilities. Work in this direction will continue.
With reference to the further observation in the report of the committee that there has not been a meeting of the federal-provincial conference on emergency measures since December, 1962, I must say this statement is correct. Now that the government has reviewed its policy and prepared a program on a basis of priorities, it is our belief that the time is opportune to hold a federal-provincial conference. I am proposing that such a conference be held in mid February of 1965. It is my belief that with adequate preparation made prior to the conference, it should be the best and most successful yet held.
It was observed also that there has been no national exercise for a number of years. It is true that the last national exercise was held in November, 1961. Preparations were made for a TOCSIN exercise in 1963, but it was not actually held. However, all studies made for the exercise, preparations and reporting, were carried through as if there had

*been an exercise. A thorough review was made of the results obtained. We are satisfied that the main aims of the exercise were met, that is, a compilation of the resources remaining at 48 hours after an attack, a review of war books and a review of emergency legislation and other similar objectives. Furthermore, studies by the provinces or by the federal emergency measures organization, in dose collaboration with the provinces, are carried on on a continuing basis. As a matter *of fact, we believe that the time has come to establish a cycle of exercises, starting at the municipal level, through to regional or provincial and finally the central level. This [DOT]allows for a much better identification and analysis of problems at each level, especially those requiring decision at the national level.
With respect to the statement in the report that this lack of continuing liaison and exercise with the provinces has seriously impaired the validity of the planning, I regret to say that I cannot entirely agree. There has been *during the period a close and continuing collaboration with the provinces although there has, as I mentioned earlier, been no formal federal-provincial conference. There has, however, been no lack of continuing discussion, [DOT]dialogue and liaison. This indeed has been sufficiently successful to warrant the holding [DOT]of the proposed federal-provincial conference next February.
Reference was made to the fact that the home shelter program has not been successful. Members of the committee will recall that this was a view put forward by the emergency measures organization itself. However, although the invitation to construct home shelters at individual expense has not been taken up by the general public, we do not believe that the government should discontinue to make available C.M.H.C. loans to those individuals who may wish to build a home shelter for their families. These, I "would remind the committee, are only loans.
No effort will be made in the future to stimulate such a program, but I believe we should make literature available to those who request it. This can be done at very little cost to the government. Already the E.M.O. has made available, in its literature, the necessary information to provide home protection [DOT]quickly with materials at hand. A pamphlet called "Simpler Shelter" is ready for distribution if the situation so warrants and the public interest demands. I believe it would be wise to continue a modest research program in this field.
Supply-Defence Production
However, the answer to the fallout problem appears to be the provision of public fallout shelters in existing buildings. Although we cannot yet evaluate the costs of modifications to buildings, on the basis of a survey completed in Alberta we can estimate that it would cost approximately 5 cents per head of the population to carry out a national fallout shelter survey across Canada, for a total of approximately $800,000.
All federal buildings have already been surveyed and over one million spaces have been identified. We are hopeful that a national survey of all large buildings will identify enough spaces to provide protection to a good percentage of the population, and this at a reasonable cost. However, before initiating such a national survey the conclusions of the Alberta survey will be very carefuly considered.
As recommended in paragraph 37, expenditures in civil emergency planning should be limited generally to priorities outlined to the special committee on defence for communications, warning system, central planning function, field co-ordinating agencies, and research on fallout and blast protection and, as stated above, fallout protection for the public if this is found to be relatively inexpensive. I can, therefore, state with confidence that the E.M.O. is in general agreement with the special committee on defence.
The staff of the organization and I were pleased to appear before the committee and would like to express our appreciation to its members for the time they devoted to this difficult but important program. I would recommend to hon. members that the estimates for E.M.O. be approved so that civil emergency planning may be adequately carried out in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there is very little time remaining this evening but I will try to condense my remarks into the period between now and ten o'clock. It seems the minister concentrated his remarks on the observations of the special committee on defence which devoted a considerable amount of time and a rather difficult chapter of its report to the difficult-because it is rather nebulous -proposition of civil defence. I say nebulous because there seems to be a lack of public consciousness of the vital necessity for civil defence.
This reminds me that during wartime there was never anything but an actual air raid, which brought air raid drill to function efficiently among units in the field, where

Supply-Defence Production one went through the experience, and all the practice you had tried to instil into yourself and your men came to the fore and they saw the value of it. The general public have a tendency to sweep the requirements of civil defence under the rug.
Several years ago when national programs of civil emergency planning were launched one of the pamphlets issued was "Eleven Steps to Survival." At that time there was a great consciousness of the necessity for civil defence, and I believe there is much to be said in favour of reviving national exercises.
I participated as a regional commissioner in both the national exercises that were held. At the beginning we were groping in the dark, with the exception of certain people involved, but by the time the second exercise was held most of the people involved had some idea what they were doing, and facilities were being prepared for them. I thought TOCSIN II accomplished a great deal, but it was held back in 1961, and a lot of the personnel involved have changed since. I would like an indication that another TOCSIN exercise will be held.
Some of the siren systems installed in certain communities seem to have been left dormant. I know other communities test their sirens every week or two at a specified time, which overcomes the nonsensical situation that occurred in Ottawa a little while ago. In fact I thought the minister should have said something to clear up that comic opera situation, when no one was home and no one could find anyone to determine why the sirens were sounding.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-QUEBEC-FEDERAL PERMISSION TO CONDUCT RAINMAKING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, I directed a question to the right hon. Prime Minister in order to find out if licences had been issued to the Weather Engineering Corporation of Canada, in Montreal for rainmaking over a given area.
I hope that tonight the Prime Minister or his representative will be in a position to tell us if individuals can take it upon themselves to throw the whole economy of an area out of gear in order to favour one sector, while we do not know on what authority they are acting and for whom.
I want this information, Mr. Speaker, because I have received numerous complaints from farmers in my constituency and in Temiscamingue and also in the light of an investigation carried out by a citizen of Rouyn, echoed in the local press, and after reading in the newspaper La Terre de Chez Nous that the Saguenay region was also being affected and that the Catholic farmers' union of that area was threatening to take legal action to protect farmers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have had a year of very bad weather in northwestern Quebec

where it rained a total of 112 days, 69 of them consecutively.
Everybody knows that agriculture is in the doldrums in eastern Canada but, in that region where normal weather conditions are not at their best, I think we should let Providence look after rainfall.
Mr. Speaker, according to some reports more than 130 of those "rainmaking machines" have been distributed across northwestern Quebec with the result that farmers in that area have been in an extremely difficult situation since the end of July. In fact, several of them will have to forsake the land unless they receive some compensation for the losses incurred as a result of rains this year.
Last year part of my region was devastated by a hurricane, a natural phenomenon; this year it was rainmaking. This doubtless, might help the forest industry by eliminating the threat of forest fires, and be of benefit to some other companies, but it is very harmful for the farmer, ever the victim.
Last year I asked for help. Nothing was granted, for Quebec did not deem it advisable to request assistance from Ottawa.
Yesterday I asked if the government would take the necessary steps to help the farmers whose crops were a failure this year, and whose lowlands, especially, have been damaged for many years to come. They did not even bother to reply.
It is easy to see that the present federal government is not the least bit interested in the welfare of eastern farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I should like the secretary to the Prime Minister to tell us, this evening, if the Weather Engineering Corporation of Canada in Montreal, operates under a federal government permit. If not, I should like the government to have an inquiry made to determine who pays that corporation and on whose behalf it is carrying out this work.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the people in the areas affected are entitled to know what is happening.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for bringing this important matter to the attention of the house. I regret my inability to reply in his native tongue, but I am sure he will understand. There are two points I wish to make in connection with the remarks of the hon. member. One was with regard to licensing. I think if anyone is licensed to operate these
Supply-Items Passed
machines which are alleged to be operating in that particular area this would be a matter for provincial jurisdiction.
Second, with regard to the question of relief for farmers who have been flooded or affected by excessive rains, this again is a provincial matter and would have to be brought by the provincial authorities to the federal government, who I am sure would be glad to assist if there is need in excess of the ability of the province to meet that need. As regards the matter of the corporation the hon. member has mentioned, I am unable to provide him with any authentic information as to whether or not this does or does not exist. I am in possession of the copy of Le Devoir from which he quoted and I am familiar with the article. I note from the article that there is no confirmation that these machines are in the area. I can only assure the hon. member that this matter will receive immediate attention and that an inquiry will be made.
